extracted.intended_audience: economists, policy makers, digital platform designers, and researchers studying blockchain economics and market design
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and criteria for analyzing how blockchain technology changes transaction costs, market structure, and platform competition; includes design considerations for tokens, consensus, governance, and real-world integration. Geared toward economic and policy assessment of blockchain-based platforms and applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of verification relates to the ability to cheaply verify state, including information about past transactions and their attributes, and current ownership in a native digital asset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower verification costs allow trust in code/consensus rather than intermediaries, enable privacy-preserving verification (e.g. zero-knowledge schemes), and let transactions be verified in real time. However, 'costless' is defined economically (not literally zero) and only applies cleanly to assets and information that are natively digital; last-mile/off-chain links remain costly. Examples: bitcoin token ownership, on-chain smart-contract state. Anti-pattern: assuming costless verification applies to offline assets without credible on-chain mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of networking
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of networking relates to the ability to bootstrap and operate a marketplace without assigning control to a centralized intermediary — i.e. the cost of bootstrapping, operating and scaling an economic network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protocols can lower networking costs by defining incentives (native tokens, mining rewards, ICOs) that reward contributions that increase adoption, security, and resources. Distinguish bootstrapping phase (incentivize early adopters/investors) from operating phase (sustain contributions, avoid tragedy of commons). Risks include speculation and attracting bad actors during bootstrapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissionless versus permissioned trust model
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the blockchain is permissionless (anyone can participate in consensus) or permissioned (access controlled) determines the trust model and whether transitions are fully self-contained in code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissionless systems replace trust in an intermediary with trust in incentives/code and lower intermediary market power; permissioned systems retain external control and operate under constraints similar to traditional platforms. Evaluate decentralization, residual rights, and reliance on formal/relational contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Last-mile / off-chain linkage (credible mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity and cost of maintaining a credible link between off-chain/real-world events (identity, physical goods, sensors) and their on-chain digital representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When off-chain attributes are easy to capture and hard to fake (e.g., diamonds' physical properties) the link is cheaper; often requires trusted intermediaries, secure IoT devices, or hardware oracles. Anti-pattern: assuming on-chain verification solves offline provenance without complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native token design and bootstrapping incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a native crypto token to create incentives for adoption, to fund development, and to reward contributors (e.g., mining rewards, ICOs, token allocations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tokens can substitute for founder/employee equity to attract talent and capital. Risks include ease of launching token sales (low barrier), regulatory uncertainty, extreme volatility driven by expectations, and attracting fraudulent projects/speculators. Evaluate token economics, distribution, and alignment of incentives across phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus and security model
rubrics_metrics.description: How the protocol secures the ledger (e.g., proof-of-work) and the dependence of security on resources dedicated to verification (e.g., computing power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sufficiency of resources to prevent attacks, susceptibility to code bugs and exploits (Parity, DAO), and tradeoffs between immutability and ability to respond to failures. Security failures can lead to forks or irreversible loss; consider attack surfaces and defense incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance and upgradeability (rule changes and forks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms for changing protocol rules, resolving disputes, and coordinating upgrades (e.g., voting processes, hard forks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes may require majority support and can cause contentious forks. Governance affects whether the system remains immutable or allows ex-post fiat editing (which undermines immutability). Evaluate governance clarity, coordination costs, and risk of contentious splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy and pseudonymity trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of transaction privacy: public/pseudonymous ledgers (Bitcoin) versus privacy-enhancing protocols (Zcash, Monero, zk-stark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privacy tech exists but pseudonymous ledgers risk deanonymization; users can take practices to protect privacy (mixers, address reuse avoidance). Consider regulatory and forensic implications, and tradeoffs between transparency for auditability and privacy for users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of intermediaries and complements
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with on-chain verification, intermediaries can add value by supporting regulatory compliance, market safety, dispute resolution, handling edge cases, and certifying off-chain information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blockchain can unbundle intermediary services, but intermediaries and secure devices often remain valuable complements. Assess which intermediary services persist and how value is reallocated (users, developers, nodes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Atomic transactions and smart contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Transactions or contracts that can be fully executed and enforced on a distributed ledger without intermediaries (atomic transactions) and programmable rules ('smart contracts').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atomicity enables escrow, verifiable gambling, token swaps, and automated settlement. For contracts depending on external data, oracles (trusted sources, aggregations, hardware) are needed; evaluate oracle trust and manipulation risk. Anti-pattern: assuming smart contracts eliminate all need for dispute mechanisms when real-world contingencies exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oracles and external data dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms to bring external (off-chain) information into smart contracts (trusted intermediaries, aggregated sources, crowdsourcing, hardware oracles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oracles are critical for derivatives, prediction markets, IoT-linked contracts. Evaluate oracle security, aggregation to avoid manipulation, and costs/availability of reliable data feeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity, credentials and provenance verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracking and verifying identities, credentials, and provenance on-chain to authenticate parties, certify attributes, and trace goods/services through supply chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blockchains can enable authentication without full disclosure and fine-grained licensing of personal data. Reliable provenance requires unique, tamper-proof fingerprints or trusted input processes (e.g., Everledger for diamonds). Evaluate privacy controls, permissioning, and need for trusted enrollment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation systems and portability
rubrics_metrics.description: Building open, verifiable reputation platforms where reviews/ratings are tied to verified transactions and portable across services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include verified reviews and reputation portability, lowering barriers to entry in markets dominated by incumbents. Assess incentives for honest reporting and privacy implications of portable reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auctions and market-design implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using distributed ledgers/smart contracts to implement auction designs that require strong commitment (e.g., second-price auctions) without exposing bids to sellers or intermediaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smart-contract auctions can ensure commitment, check bidder funding, and destroy losing bids. Evaluate whether on-chain mechanisms restore implementability of theoretically efficient auction formats and prevent expropriation or strategic leakage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central bank digital currency (CBDC) implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential for central banks to issue fiat-backed digital currency on blockchain-like infrastructure, with implications for commercial banks, taxation, monetary policy, and traceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how costless verification would reshape tax enforcement and money supply operations; evaluate political/regulatory tradeoffs and effects on private-sector services (wallet security, payment innovation).

rubrics_metrics.name: IoT and secure hardware as complements
rubrics_metrics.description: Role of Internet-of-Things devices and secure sensors in expanding contracts that can be automated by reliably capturing real-world data (e.g., GPS, weather sensors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure hardware reduces off-chain verification costs and enables markets for energy, bandwidth, and device-to-device transactions. Evaluate hardware tamper-resistance, incentives for truthful reporting, and integration costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-good nature of protocol layer and governance funding
rubrics_metrics.description: The protocol layer is a shared public good; improvements benefit all but may be underprovided without governance/funding mechanisms, risking a tragedy of the commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess mechanisms to fund public-good investments (protocol upgrades, security improvements), token economics that sustain long-term contributions, and institutional arrangements to avoid underinvestment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unbundling of intermediary services and impact on incumbents
rubrics_metrics.description: Reductions in verification costs allow previously bundled intermediary services to be separated and collectively managed by ecosystem stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect incumbents to retain roles in compliance and safety; evaluate which services are displaced versus which persist as paid-added services. Consider competition effects and rent allocation among users, developers, and nodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granularity of property rights and micropayments
rubrics_metrics.description: Blockchain enables defining property rights at very granular scales (small fractions of assets) and low-friction micropayments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can change pricing, advertising, and content monetization (e.g., micro-payments in browsers). Evaluate transaction costs, on-chain fees, and whether granularity creates novel markets or complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-of-existence / timestamping (first-to-file)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a blockchain to record hashes/digital fingerprints as immutable timestamps to prove existence or priority (first-to-file) without revealing underlying data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for IP claims, lab notes, and timestamped evidence. Note loss risk if private record is destroyed; public ledger only stores proof, not content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-chain/aggregated settlement and privacy tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some providers perform off-chain transactions (recording aggregate inputs/outputs) to improve privacy and scalability at the cost of centralization and trust in the provider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess privacy benefits vs. added privacy risk from centralized providers and loss of on-chain auditability. Evaluate tradeoffs in security, censorship resistance, and regulatory oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and compliance constraints (KYC/AML)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal and regulatory frictions (e.g., KYC/AML) that limit adoption, especially where linking on-chain identities to offline identities is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when on-chain verification is low-cost, compliance may impose additional costs to credibly link identities; evaluate jurisdictional constraints and how they affect feasible use-cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volatility, speculation, and information-friction risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Token valuations are often driven by expectations about future success, leading to high volatility, bubbles, and difficulty distinguishing high-quality projects from fraudulent/speculative ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how speculative dynamics affect capital allocation, crowding out of R&D, investor protection, and long-term project viability. Anti-pattern: equating large token market cap with technological maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code-bug and fraud vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk that programming mistakes, deliberate fraud (e.g., ICO scams), or malicious attacks exploit protocol or application code leading to losses or forks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate code audits, formal verification, bug-bounty practices, legal recourse limits, and contingency plans (e.g., hard forks). Historical examples: Parity library removal, DAO hack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sousveillance and embedded auditability
rubrics_metrics.description: Blockchain can embed audit capabilities in marketplace rules (sousveillance), enabling frequent, fine-grained verification and reducing need for costly external audits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can improve transparency and accountability but may raise privacy concerns. Assess which audit functions can be on-chain and the residual role of auditors for complex or off-chain issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interoperability, standards, and open-source commons
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared ledgers and protocol-level rules function like standards; open-source foundations and collaboration among competitors shape governance and interoperability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate standard-setting dynamics, ease of forking/imitating codebases, and implications for competition. Consider how open governance affects innovation diffusion and coordination.
